title: About Technology - Intro
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Martin Skelton opens his series on technology as a factor that affects learning by restating his definition of learning as a good struggle that changes neural chains, then judging technology against it. He tells the story of a film-strip geography teacher whose clumsy use of a projector wasted lessons and taught students negative things, to show that technology is old news and is inert until a person uses it. He admits that enthusiasts, himself included, can make technology their Hedgehog Concept, while apprehensive teachers are sometimes right to be wary. He reviews Brookings, J-PAL, the House of Lords and the EEF and concludes the evidence points to benefits and risks but is too small-scale, too contested and too quickly outdated by AI to give firm classroom guidance. He recasts benefits and risks as good learning and bad learning and previews two follow-up posts.
points: Technology is treated as a neutral tool whose value depends on the user's skill and purpose, illustrated by a film strip that cost three lessons of learning time.
Skelton warns that enthusiasm for gadgets can become a school's or teacher's real purpose, displacing learning itself.
His reading of Brookings, J-PAL, the House of Lords and the EEF is that the research supports benefits and risks alike but is thought-provoking rather than practically decisive.
Covid and unequal access raise the concern that technology can widen learning gaps while helping some students.
He proposes reframing benefits and risks as good learning and bad learning, noting that today's poor technology experiences are far harder to escape than a single dull lesson.
quotes: I have learned that each piece of technology is inert, neither good nor bad. Like every tool, it is only as good as the person using it and the reasons they are using it.

This state of the art film strip projector combined with a dull set of pictures and someone who both loved the sound of his own voice and couldn’t master the technology had a negative impact on both our immediate learning and, over the long term, what we thought about both geography and about Mr Warburton. Our stories about him and his wasted lessons were already adding to many other similar stories that circulated around the school.
For some of us, dangerously, technology has become our Hedgehog Concept: ‘Look at my students using all this new stuff. Look at me using it, too. Aren’t we all modern and up to date?

Technology is provoking discussion and arguments, too, about its impact on the mental health children and students. There is a great deal of opinion - from me, too, just to say - but the evidence base isn’t yet secure.

Here’s the Covid issue writ large. Is technology helping some children and students learn better whilst at the same time increasing the gap between those who can benefit from access to technology and those who aren’t so lucky?

In truth, much of the current research evidence is thought-provoking, helping us decide in which directions we need to look and reflect on, rather than practically useful, giving us clear guidance about what to do in our classrooms and schools next week. There are a number of reasons for this.

The difference now is that many technologies involved in learning are available freely to everyone, at any time. We could, forty minutes later, escape from Mr. Warburton’s unhelpful learning lessons. It’s much harder to escape now.
